en: The Annotated Explanation of the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
Scroll One,
Compiled by the Monk Doyin, Imperial Preceptor for Discourse on the Imperial Retinue.
I prostrate to the Sugata, the Great Sage Hero, Who is fully endowed with wisdom, abandonment, compassion, and all virtues;
To him who expounds the vajra words of purity, Whose principles are profound and whose merit is wondrous beyond thought.
I prostrate to the Venerable Subhūti, the Honored One, Who was able to make his request at that time and who contemplates emptiness.
The Bodhisattvas currently abiding in the stage of succession, those in the Stage of Extreme Joy, and those in the Stage of Increasing Radiance—

may all who expound this teaching now, for the sake of generating merit and wisdom for themselves and others, gather the meaning of the Dharma that sustains the lineage of the Buddhas and causes it to flow forth,
and praise these true words. May they be granted protection through their majestic spiritual power.
The Preface states:
The true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is vast and empty;
the principle is profound and obscure, and awakening is deep and mysterious.
Fundamentally, there is no discourse;
yet one gives rise to speech within the realm of the unspeakable,
and establishes names within the sphere of the nameless.
This is truly because the dark path has not yet dawned;
seeing the vast ocean of long-standing discourse,
I shall employ this lamp and torch.
The ferry across the dark pass and the crossing of the strait:
such is the flourishing of the teaching for all classes of beings.
How great indeed is its merit!
How much more so the Prajñāpāramitā, the mother of all Buddhas,
the indestructible words of the Vajra,
which stands alone, encompassing all sections.
Crowning all the scriptures, it soars far aloft;
through three questions and nine parables,
it elucidates from beginning to end the eight attachments and five errors.
When the mind and its expressions are utterly extinguished, and one is protected by mindfulness and entrusted with the teaching,
how could the Way be something practiced in vain?
During the Kaiyuan era of the Great Tang,
in the twenty-third year of Emperor Xuanhuang’s reign over the empire,
the four gates were harmonious and peaceful.
The hundred officials were well-ordered;
the supreme transformation permeated the boundless reaches,
and the profound wind flourished throughout all lands.
Thereupon, he concentrated his sagely reflections and eloquently expounded upon Confucianism and Daoism,
while still cherishing the wondrous awakening of the Buddha.
The commentary and esoteric instructions on this sutra directly illuminate its subtle essence and fully reveal its secrets.
The celestial edicts radiate brilliance;
the Buddha-sun increases its luster.
Illuminating the ages past as preeminent, it transcends a hundred kings to provide a lasting model.
Subsequently, at the capital, the imperial seat,
[the stele] was engraved upon metal and stone;
throughout the heavens and across all lands, [it was proclaimed].
Proclaiming the words and their meanings,
it cleanses the ears and eyes of living beings and tears asunder the cages and enclosures of demonic attachments.
Not encountered throughout vast eons,
how fortunate I am today!
Yet I lie prostrate, ill within the forest thickets.
Having followed the traces of Du for many years,
I have humbly perused the sagely counsels and felt a surge of joyful anticipation.
I have now received the gracious imperial decree.
Having presumptuously joined in the propagation [of the Dharma],
I have exerted my efforts to diligently expound the profound and abstruse traces, despite being but a remnant of the weary and decrepit.
My talent is meager yet the responsibility is heavy;
my failure to manage the stew has increased my faults. On this occasion of occupying this seat, how could I fear prolixity? I humbly consider that when the sovereign initiates, the minister responds.
The movement of the wheel proceeds from a single strand;
if one does not extensively cite scriptural texts,
how can this be explained in detail?
He paid close attention to their application,
synthesizing various treatises and correlating them with the Six Classics.
Emerging spontaneously from his lips,
it was manifested in his brushwork;
he suddenly cast aside his rhinoceros-hide armor and ivory tusks to yield his fangs and horns.
To encompass rivers and marshes to offer up pearls and treasures is to supplement the celestial patterns and adorn the treasury of meaning; yet as a mere drop of water flows into the sea,
how could it increase the depth of the vast ocean?
A firefly or a torch displaying its light cannot assist the splendor of the sun;
yet I respectfully present this boundless offering to humbly manifest my loyalty and diligence.
The commentary on the title of the sutra is divided into four parts.
First, the explanation of the metaphor:
that is, the adamantine, true jewel.
It can shatter solid accumulations.
Second is the wisdom of liberation,
which is precisely the right wisdom of *prajñā*.
It is able to destroy afflictions.
Third is the exposition of its qualities:
namely, non-abiding and non-appropriation.
Having realized the *pāramitā*, one abandons the raft;
realizing that form is emptiness,
one accords with *bodhi* in the Middle Way.
Fourth, the explanation of the sūtra:
that is, subduing in this manner can be called "constant."
Therefore, it is called the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
In this commentary extolling the sūtra,
I shall briefly open five gates.
First, an account of the causes for the arising of the teaching;
second, an elucidation of the essence and nature of the sūtra;
third, a summary that brings it back to its fundamental tenets.
Fourth, the suitability of the faculties for whom the teaching is intended;
fifth, the correct interpretation based on the text;
and sixth, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching.
The composition is divided into two sections:
first, an account of the intent behind the emergence of the teaching;
second, the chronology of its transmission and translation.
The beginning and middle further consist of two parts:
first, an explanation based on the treatise;
second, a general summary and analysis.
Regarding the commentary on the treatise:
the Bodhisattva Asaṅga explains the intent of the three questions.
The treatise asks: "For what reason, Elder Subhūti?"
As for why this question was raised,
there are six causes and conditions.
First, regarding the fundamental tenet of this treatise:
The matter rests upon these three questions;
Subhūti serves as the master who initiates the teaching.
Since he possesses this intention, [the Buddha speaks].
The World-Honored One inquired accordingly;
since the intent of the response must necessarily be the same,
the six conditions constitute the purpose for the arising of the teaching.
What are these six?
The treatise states:
"In order to sever doubt."
For the sake of giving rise to faith and understanding;
for the sake of entering into the profound meaning;
and for the sake of non-retrogression.
For the sake of generating joy,
and for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma,
this is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā.
It causes the lineage of the Buddhas not to be severed.
How does this cause the lineage of the Buddhas not to be severed?
Should there be any doubt on this matter:
Because they have attained the severance of doubt,
they possess the joy of merit,
yet their minds are not yet matured.
Because the various bodhisattvas,
upon hearing that the merit in the Prajñāpāramitā is vast,
give rise to faith and understanding.
One whose mind has already been matured enters into the profound meaning;
one who has already attained it is no longer subject to contempt.
By receiving, upholding, and practicing out of desire,
there are many merits,
for one will no longer regress.
For those who have already attained compliance, integration, and a pure mind,
because they enter into the Dharma spontaneously and experience joy upon seeing it,
they are able to [bring about] future lives.
Because the Mahāyāna teachings are to abide for a long time.
The commentary states:
"The first five are for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings."
The last one is for the long endurance of the True Dharma.
Among the first five,
the first two—
Those outside the Buddha-dharma harbor doubts and do not give rise to certain faith; this refers to the next two [categories].
Those who have already entered the Buddha-dharma,
though they rejoice in the True Dharma,
have not yet understood how to advance in their practice.
As for the latter, those who have already engaged in cultivation have not yet attained realization;
the teaching serves merely to provide understanding for those who do not yet understand.
Those who have not yet crossed over are delivered.
Once realization has been attained,
all verbal teachings vanish.
Therefore, herein, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings who lack faith to have faith,
and those who have not yet practiced to practice.
Those who have not yet attained reach attainment.
Furthermore, these six causes are subsumed into three pairs.
The first two [pairs] correspond to the removal of doubt and the arousal of faith;
the next two correspond to the generation of wisdom and the gathering of merit;
the final two correspond to the realization of principle and the manifestation of the teaching.
Furthermore, each preceding cause is able to induce each succeeding cause;
because doubt is severed, resolute faith arises.
Because faith and understanding arise, one enters the profound Dharma.
Because one enters the profound Dharma, one does not regress.
Because one does not regress, joy arises.
Because of joy, the Dharma abides for a long time.
As for the arrangement of their positions,
it shall be explained when the relevant passage is reached.
Furthermore, according to the *Guṇaprabha-bodhisattva-śāstra*, it is said:
"All the teachings expounded by the Buddha ultimately converge upon the two truths."
First is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
and second is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
As for the conventional truth:
That is to say, all ordinary persons,
śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
Bodhisattvas [know] the Tathāgata’s sphere of knowledge regarding names and meanings,
as well as the interconnectedness of karma and its results.
Yan said: "Within the conventional truth,
persons and phenomena are distinct."
Among humans, there are both the ordinary and the noble; among the noble, there are those of the three vehicles;
and within the Mahāyāna, there are cause and fruit.
Within such differentiated phenomena,
there are the signifier and the signified, as well as the subject that cognizes and the object that is cognized.
That which causes and that which is caused are each mutually interconnected;
this is called conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
The treatise further states:
"Ultimate truth" refers to the fact that,
within this very [reality], nothing at all can be apprehended.
As it is said: "The ultimate truth is not within the range of cognition,
let alone that of words."
"Up to the point where there is neither karma nor the fruit of karma, such is the lineage of the noble ones (*āryagotra*).
Having thus explained the two truths, the treatise proceeds to correlate them with the following passage from the Sūtra:
Therefore, in this Prajñāpāramitā,
it is taught that one should not abide in signs; all dharmas are signless.
It is ungraspable and ineffable;
the nature of arising phenomena is selflessness.
There is nothing to be attained;
there is nothing to be realized;
there is nothing to be accomplished.
"Neither coming nor going," and so forth;
this explains the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Furthermore, it speaks of the internal and external.
The characteristics of all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane,
as well as all their merits.
This establishes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
It should be understood in this way.
[The commentary] states:
Beyond the six sense objects and within the five eyes;
beyond form and within the mind.
Sentient beings and their environment constitute the world.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) constitute the supramundane.
Taken together, these are designated as the characteristics of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-lakṣaṇa*).
The intent of the treatise is to weigh and compare the life-span and material wealth [of others] with the merit of upholding this sutra and other such virtues.
Sentient beings do not recognize the two truths and thus constantly remain mired in saṃsāra;
in order to cause sentient beings to recognize and penetrate the two truths, [the Buddha taught this].
Supreme wisdom arises,
and one shall attain liberation.
As it is said in a verse:
It is not that one fails to perceive suchness,
yet is able to understand that all conditioned phenomena are like illusory beings and the like.
Although they exist, they are not real;
by contemplating the ultimate truth (paramārtha),
correct wisdom (samyagjñāna) arises.
By awakening to ultimate emptiness,
one realizes conventional reality; through this attainment, subsequent knowledge arises,
whereby one understands dependent origination.
Briefly, there are six pairs:
the wisdom of principle and the wisdom of phenomena; the wisdom of reality and the wisdom of events.
The knowledge of all things, the knowledge of all aspects,
and the wisdom that is like awakening from a dream.
The wisdom like the blooming lotus,
the wisdom of emptiness,
and the wisdom of existence.
Wisdom for one's own benefit,
wisdom for the benefit of others,
and wisdom regarding the nature of things as they are.
The knowledge of the full extent of all things (*yāvadbhāvikajñāna*) and the immeasurable merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
these two types of knowledge are the fundamental cause; because one realizes the ultimate and conventional truths, this knowledge arises.
Therefore, the sutras are taught to bring about the realization of the two truths.
Furthermore, by virtue of realizing the ultimate truth,
wisdom arises and one does not abide in saṃsāra.
Because of the realization of the conventional,
one gives rise to compassion and does not abide in nirvāṇa;
or rather, this constitutes the provisions for non-abiding nirvāṇa.
It is taught as a sutra because it brings about eternal transcendence from the two vehicles and provides inexhaustible benefit and happiness.
The above is an explanation based on the treatise.
Next, regarding the general summary:
Bodhisattva Asaṅga, relying on the teachings, gave rise to practice,
as explained in the *Guṇaprabha-śāstra*.
Cognition arises based on its respective objects; each [explanation] relies on a single specific meaning,
and thus they do not contradict one another.
However, when the sutras and śāstras are examined in their entirety from the first to the sixth [chapter],
their intended meaning is fully encompassed.
As for the "single meaning," it is for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Buddha is not severed.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga summarizes the six causes, stating:
"This is precisely the Prajñāpāramitā,
which ensures that the Buddhas are never interrupted."
If this intention is overturned by the six causes of doubt, such as non-abiding and so forth, superior wisdom will not arise;
reality will not be revealed,
and the lineage of the Buddha will be permanently severed.
By means of expounding the sutras,
doubts are removed, faith is generated,
and one enters the Dharma without falling back.
Rejoicing in its widespread propagation,
one shall attain perfect enlightenment;
therefore, it is said that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
Regarding the statement "the meaning of the two," this refers to the two truths discussed in the preceding treatise;
these are opened up to become three.
First, to realize the profound and subtle nature of the teachings and principles;
second, to give rise to the wondrous practices of abandonment and cultivation;
third, to recognize the true manifestations of the virtues of the fruition.
The first gate further consists of two parts:
first, the profundity of the teaching;
second, the subtlety of the principle.
Regarding the profundity of the teaching:
the Buddha said that "Prajñāpāramitā" is not actually Prajñāpāramitā.
All Buddhas are born from this sutra.
Subhūti, having deeply understood its meaning and intent,
wept with tears of sorrow.
Since ancient times, regarding the eye of wisdom I have attained,
I have never before heard [of such a thing].
Regarding such a sutra, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states:
"It causes the Mahāyāna teaching to abide long in the world."
By this, the excellence of the merit of upholding and expounding [the teaching] is extensively praised;
through the giving of immeasurable bodies and wealth, one causes others to know the profundity of the instruction.
This merit is vast and supreme, and thus one should study with single-minded devotion.
The phrase "the subtlety of principle" is used to manifest the principle of the ultimate Dharmakāya, which is the signless True Suchness (tathatā).
Although ultimate truth is taught,
it does not subvert conventional truth;
thus, it is the *Guṇaprabha-śāstra*.
The name is established based on the sūtras;
by destroying grasping and attachment,
one attains entry into ultimate truth.
Without destroying conventional designations,
one awakens to and attains the mundane truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As stated in the tenth chapter of the *Śata-śāstra*:
Nevertheless, there is nothing among the Buddha’s teachings that is not profoundly deep;
the dharma-gate of the two truths is the most difficult to fathom.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"To deny the two truths is to engage in a perverted grasping of emptiness (*durgṛhītaśūnyatā*)."
The Buddhas declare such persons to be incurable.
For this reason, some say that the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras teach that all things are empty.
This does not exhaust the principle.
Second, the arising of the sublime practices of abandonment and cultivation is also twofold.
First, that which is abandoned;
second, that which is cultivated.
Regarding the term "that which is abandoned":
Those who wish to enter the Buddha-dharma must take faith as their priority;
yet they remain hesitant and harbor doubts.
While the *Dharmāvatāra-śāstra* explains the principle of severing doubt as the basis for generating pure faith,
this sutra additionally severs other obstacles.
There are two kinds of obstructions:
those of afflictions and those of the cognizable.
If one seeks their root source, [one finds...]
The two types of grasping are the root.
This sutra correctly eliminates these two graspings for self and phenomena;
once the root is exhausted, [the afflictions are likewise eliminated].
The branches and extremities perish accordingly.
As the Sūtra says: "If there is the mark of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, then one is not a bodhisattva," and so forth.
This eliminates the grasping at a self;
that there is neither the mark of dharmas nor the mark of non-dharmas eliminates the grasping at dharmas.
Furthermore, there are three obstructions,
namely the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
When I was previously being dismembered limb by limb, [I felt no resentment].
If there is the mark of a self,
the mark of a person,
or the mark of a sentient being.
One who perceives a self in terms of lifespan should give rise to anger and so forth; thus,
one eliminates the afflictive obstructions.
If good sons or good daughters accept,
uphold, read, and recite this sutra,
they will be treated with contempt by others.
"Karmic offenses from previous lives shall be immediately extinguished," and so forth;
thus their karmic obstacles are eliminated.
One should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable,
and its karmic fruit and retribution are likewise inconceivable;
this eliminates the obstacle of retribution.
Furthermore, according to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*,
there are four kinds of obstacles: first,
the lack of faith of the icchantika.
Second, non-Buddhists are attached to a self;
third, śrāvakas fear suffering;
fourth, pratyekabuddhas abandon the mind [of compassion].
Now, within this sutra,
by taking the meaning according to the text,
one fully eliminates the four obstacles.
As it is said: "One who has given rise to pure faith for even a single moment has long planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas."
"Faith and purity of mind lead to the arising of the true mark," and so forth;
these are all obstacles at the initial stage.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"There are those who possess merit and happiness,
yet whose minds are not yet matured."
Because the bodhisattvas, upon hearing of the great merit, give rise to faith and understanding in the *prajñāpāramitā*,
the sūtra text— both preceding and following—
speaks of non-self and so forth.
To eliminate the second hindrance:
the perfection of patience is,
in itself, not the perfection of patience, and so forth.
In the treatise, this is judged to be the dwelling place for enduring suffering;
it removes the third hindrance and is vast and foremost.
By maintaining a mind that is constant and free from inversion,
one cultivates the fourfold mind of gratitude and removes the fourth hindrance.
If one delights in inferior teachings,
then one will be unable to receive, read, recite,
or explain them to others from the sutras.
Furthermore, regarding the passage on non-abiding nirvāṇa,
it generally excludes the latter two [of the three types of nirvāṇa].
Moreover, according to the eight bases of dwelling (*āśraya*) set forth by the Bodhisattva Asanga:
These twelve factors are subsumed under "removal of obstacles.
Each is paired with a specific hindrance to be eliminated, such as limited learning and so forth;
it is for the purpose of removing these obstacles that this sutra is taught.
Regarding the second point, those who practice:
although the myriad practices differ, they do not exceed the six perfections.
As Vasubandhu’s treatise states:
The perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) comprises material goods, fearlessness,
and the Dharma; herein, the first, second,
and third are called the stages of abiding in practice.
Furthermore, the relinquishing of one's body, wealth, and so forth constitutes *dāna* (generosity);
in the final five hundred years,
the upholding of the precepts and the cultivation of merit and so forth constitute *śīla* (ethical discipline).
Furthermore, apart from all characteristics and so forth,
it includes the precepts of restraint (saṃvara-śīla),
the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas, the attainment of unexcelled bodhi, and so on.
The precept for gathering wholesome dharmas,
and the precept for gathering sentient beings for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings and so forth—
these are the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*).
Furthermore, the three types of generating the mind of awakening— which involve yoga and revulsion toward the conditioned and so forth— are the causes for the three virtues;
this is called ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Patience can be understood through this:
it was practiced for a long duration throughout five hundred lifetimes.
This constitutes diligence.
Regarding the contemplative practices cultivated throughout the preceding and subsequent passages:
The treatise judges that *samāpatti*, *vipaśyanā*,
and so forth constitute the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*).
The six perfections are fulfilled.
At the end of the Great Sūtra, the six are clarified as the pāramitās;
this is a brief enumeration intended to indicate that the cultivation of signlessness gives rise to what follows.
Third, regarding those who are true transformations of the merit that is the fruit of consciousness:
although Subhūti’s three questions pertain to the causal stage,
the cause must necessarily lead to the unsurpassed fruit.
Seeking me through forms and sounds,
you do not see that the Tathāgata is the true Dharma-body;
walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are the response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
The manifested transformation body is not the true Buddha,
nor is it the speaker of the Dharma; this is intended to make known the nature of the transformation body.
Seeking to attain the true Buddha.
Furthermore, the *Guṇaprabha-śāstra-vyākhyā* asks:
"What is meant by 'abiding'?"
In what kind of signs and fruits does the mind abide and aspire?
How should a practitioner practice,
and what conduct should they cultivate to attain those fruits?
What is meant by "subduing"?
It is to subdue the mind so that its causes become pure.
All phenomena have their cause first and their fruit later.
Why are the fruits explained first?
It is because one first praises the virtues of the fruit so that others may aspire to them and cultivate the causes.
In the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, Maitreya Bodhisattva distinguishes three types of causes, whose principles encompass both practice and fruit.
Regarding the second point, the objects of the two truths pervade both the fruit and the cause; this concludes the three meanings.
To expand these into four:
first, it is to enable the hearing of the unsurpassed teaching that is beyond verbal expression.
Second, it is to cause [beings] to know the supreme principle of non-arising;
third, it is to cause them to cultivate the wondrous practice of non-attainment;
fourth, it is to cause them to attain the ultimate fruit of the unconditioned.
It is exactly as stated in the sutra;
one should seek out and cite it.
If one were to expand upon these five points:
To these four, one further adds [two more],
in order to ensure the acquisition of the wondrous merit of signlessness (*animitta*).
As for the "six intentions":
This explains the six causes of affliction;
that is, within each of the three aforementioned categories,
they are each divided into two.
First, the teaching;
second, the principle;
third, the abandonment.
Fourth, cultivation;
fifth, reality;
sixth, transformation.
Therefore, based on the general intent of the sūtras and śāstras, I desire to eliminate doubts,
sever hindrances, engender faith, initiate practice,
and discern the principles of the ultimate and conventional truths.
Gathering the virtues of merit and wisdom,
one realizes the fruit of the Dharma-body,
ensuring that the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted.
This sutra originated thus.
To clarify the dates of its transmission and translation:
it began with Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty’s dream-vision.
After Matanga shook his monk’s staff and An Shigao hastened to Luoyang,
and before Kang Senghui traveled to Wu.
Although these subtle words had spread throughout the Central States,
this scripture had not yet circulated within the land of China;
it was only from the time of the Fu Qin dynasty that it began.
Reaching the era of the Imperial Destiny, the time for its universal response arrived.
In total, there were six translations.
The first was in the fourth year of the Hongshi era of the Later Qin.
The Dharma Master Kumārajīva translated eleven sheets titled "The City of Śrāvastī" at Cāotáng Monastery in Chāng'ān.
The second [translation] was by Yuánwèi during the second year of the Tiān píng era.
The Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci translated fourteen sheets titled *Bhagavat* at Luoyang;
at that time, he also translated three fascicles of the treatise by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.
*Vajrasattva-ācārya-carita*, ten fascicles.
Third: Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha in the first year of the Taikang era of the Chen dynasty.
In the Southern Dynasty, fifteen sheets were translated, titled *Jītavana-vana* (The Jeta Grove),
along with a four-fascicle original preface (*benji*).
Fourth, in the tenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
Dharmagupta translated sixteen sheets titled *Gangduange* (The Firm Severing),
as well as two fascicles of the treatise by Bodhisattva Asanga.
Fifth was the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.
During the Zhenguan era,
at Yuhua Palace, he translated the eighteen-folio work titled *Nengduan jingang* (The Diamond Cutter that Can Sever).
There was also the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara.
This is titled *Zhao Ri* (Sunlight).
It is a two-fascicle translation of the *Bodhisattva-guṇaprabha-śāstra*.
The sixth [entry] is by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing of the Great Zhou.
In the second year of the Shengli era, it was translated at Foshouji Monastery in twelve sheets of paper; it is also called *Nengduan Jingang* (The Diamond that Can Sever).
The text states: "The Bhagavat was in the city of Yaśovatī, in the Vijayārāma, and so forth."
He also retranslated three fascicles of the treatise by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva;
thus, the transmission of the lamp was maintained from beginning to end, bringing glory to both eras.
Although the phrasing differs slightly,
there is no discrepancy in the Dharma-treasure;
this is truly because of the Sanskrit manuscripts from which they were obtained.
There are mutual differences among them;
some were translated by different individuals,
resulting in variations in detail and brevity.
One should cross-reference them with one another so that the principles and meanings may be fully realized.
This is especially true when the sūtras and śāstras are presented together.
Thus, Zhou and Wei each have their own divisions;
yet, as long as the Chinese and Sanskrit do not fall into deficiency, the *Zhenguan* [era] version is the most complete.
As for the brevity of expression and clarity of meaning, it accords with the capacities of beings and responds to their conditions.
That its transcription fills the entire world and its recitation pervades both the monastic and lay communities—
this can only be expected of the Kingdom of Śrāvastī.
The glorious radiance of the holy texts must surely reside herein.
Therefore, I have now appended the commentaries of the Sui and Wei dynasties to the scriptures of the Yao Qin.
Question:
The original sūtra can be known; as for the various treatises, I shall now set forth their authors. Answer:
Nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
As for their secular relationship, Asanga was a noble being of the first bhūmi,
while Vasubandhu was a great scholar at the stages of uṣmagata and mūrdhan; they were brothers.
The Dharma is the foundation for both teacher and disciple;
each shall compose treatises to praise and propagate this scripture.

Because of the purity of the wisdom and vision that penetrates selflessness;
because it is not the grasping of a mind abiding in signs;
and because the essence of the reality of all phenomena is unconditioned.
Because merit and wisdom are like space and incalculable, they correspond to the ten preceding metaphors;
thus they are explained through this allocation.
Although the meaning is complete herein, [the text continues].
This is not the intended meaning of the treatise.

Now, [the practitioner] is able to maintain the three types of wisdom and to eliminate the two obstacles.

both are termed "vajra.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
The adamantine is extremely firm; no thing can destroy or remove it.

Using the horns of a white sheep and the shell of a tortoise as metaphors for the two obstacles, according to their respective applications, these cannot be severed by ordinary beings or those of the Two Vehicles.
Only by generating the great bodhicitta can one subdue it through the three types of wisdom; otherwise,
this [affliction] must be severed, for what is to be severed is likened to a vajra, like entering into the practice of false views.
Furthermore, just as the nature of jade and stone is extremely firm and cannot be destroyed by any other object,
only the vajra is able to crush and break it.
The two obstacles are likewise so.

They cannot be destroyed by the mundane wisdom of ordinary beings or the true knowledge of the followers of the Two Vehicles, because the Two Vehicles do not sever the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the obstacles of afflictions. Only the three types of wisdom of the Mahāyāna—like that diamond (*vajra*)—are able to subdue and sever them; this refers to the stage of ultimate severance, which is the diamond-like cultivation-wisdom (*vajropama-bhāvanā-prajñā*). Therefore, the Sūtra speaks only of the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*). This very [concentration] is the metaphor for the diamond, as it enters into the practice of right view; thus, it is said to have two meanings.
First is the meaning of that which is destroyed;
second is the meaning of that which destroys.

If it were only the meaning of destroying, the analogy would be inconsistent with both the false and the correct views. However, the treatise is concise and does not explicitly explain this. Within the context of "that which cuts," the *vajra* (diamond/thunderbolt) is implicitly contained and only then revealed. Furthermore, the explanation of the *vajra* merely serves as an analogy for the three benefits and the teaching.
The reason for this is stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "It is,
for example, like a vajra, which is extremely hard."
Nothing can damage it,
except for the tortoise shell and so forth;
that sūtra is also like this.
Except for those who have abandoned all hope (icchantikas),
it cannot cause them to establish the causes for awakening;
they are like the horns of a sheep and so forth.
Using this as a metaphor for the icchantika,
it clarifies that they are not subject to severance;
thus, it is named "vajra."
As for the statement regarding two meanings:
first, the realization of the principle of *tathatā* (suchness),
as in the practice of entering into right view.
Second, it severs all delusions;
it is like entering into the practice of false views—
this adamantine wisdom.
It can destroy the two layers of obstructive afflictions in those who possess roots of goodness within the Mahāyāna and whose faculties have matured;
however, it cannot eliminate the afflictions within the persons of those who have severed their roots of goodness.
For this reason, another explanation states:

According to this treatise, the first section on the "Cluster of Meanings of the Indestructible Vajra Phrase" clarifies that [the afflictions] are not what is to be severed. Although there are other passages stating that the afflictions are difficult to sever, being like a vajra, the present context asserts that they *can* be severed; thus, it is inappropriate to employ the vajra as a metaphor here. This is similar to how the icchantika is said to be difficult to transform by using the metaphor of parched grain, whereas when it is said that the icchantika can be cured, this metaphor is not used. Regarding the statement that the two meanings correspond: the vajra is able to sever both hard and non-hard objects; these are called the "two meanings. The commentary states:

The initial explanation is superior because it accords with the treatise; thus, by means of the diamond-like simile, it characterizes both the wisdom that is capable [of cutting] and the obstacles to be severed, thereby manifesting the function of that wisdom.
The *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*, in its second chapter, states:

How is the continuity [of defilements] destroyed? Just as there are many paths according to the principle of the vajra-like afflictions (*kleśa*), how could their metaphors be fixed? For example, while space is used as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), it is also used as a metaphor for the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*). Coarse gold is cited in the *Nyāyamukha* (The Gate of Logic) because it serves as a gateway for both wisdom and insight; the obstructions are said to be difficult to sever, being like vajra, to manifest that the power of wisdom is supreme and transcendent. Since nothing can truly serve as a metaphor for that which is beyond metaphor, why would one insist on contemplating the hardness of the afflictions in order to give rise to the practice of contemplation?
If that is so, how should one reconcile the fact that the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the analogies of the ram's horns and so forth are inconsistent? Answer:
The meaning of the text regarding *nirvāṇa* does not explain this sutra;
I now borrow that analogy for present purposes.
This is to manifest the diamond (vajra).

These two substances are used as metaphors for the objects that obstruct; they represent the "antidotes" (*pratipakṣa*) and do not refer to the obstructions to nirvāṇa. Regarding the diamond, the upper section explains it in terms of both the subject that cuts and the object that is cut, while the lower section provides a specific interpretation focusing solely on the subject that cuts, which possesses four meanings.
As listed previously,
the treatise states:
"The subtle [factors] are the cause of wisdom."

"Solid" (*lao*) means that which cannot be destroyed; because the Sui dynasty tabooed the character for "hard" (*jian*), it was translated as "subtle" (*xi*). This takes up the sense of being firm and dense.

The cause of wisdom is the seed, and that which cannot be destroyed is the manifest activity (*samudācāra*). Because wisdom transcends delusion and eliminates it—such that light and darkness do not coexist—it cannot be destroyed. Furthermore, another explanation is that wisdom is able to realize *tathatā* (suchness) by virtue of its nature as a "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*), and is thus called the "cause of wisdom. Because it is without gaps and is not interspersed with worldly activities, it is termed "subtle and dense" (*sūkṣma-gāḍha*). Moreover, because it is subtle and wondrous, it is not an object of perception for the coarse [minds] of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); thus, these two names signify "subtle and dense. As for the phrase "cannot be destroyed," it reveals that the nature of the obstacles to be remedied is so firm that they are difficult to destroy. According to this interpretation, the four meanings within the treatise apply to both the subject that cuts and the objects that are cut.
The treatise further states:

"That which is capable of severing [the afflictions] does so by means of the severance achieved through hearing, reflection, and cultivation within the Prajñāpāramitā, like the point at which a diamond cuts. Thus, because wisdom is like a diamond, it is able to sever the two obstacles; these [obstacles], being like jade or stone, are termed 'points of severance.'"
In the former case, one cites that which is severed to reveal that which severs;
if one were to interpret the diamond as a metaphor for the two obstacles,
this would cite that which severs to reveal that which is severed.

It is "like a vajra" in the sense that the obstacles to be abandoned through hearing, reflection, and cultivation are severed with the same decisiveness as a vajra cuts through its object; according to the intent of the treatise, this explains the title *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, which is indicated at the outset by the term "vajra-cutter," and is further concluded later by the statement, "this is called the Vajracchedikā."
The same applies within the commentary: first the Vajra is explained, and subsequently the "ability to sever" is explained; this accords with the terminology of the Western Regions (India).
If one were to say "the Vajra that severs," it would accord with the terminology of this region (China).
None of these are mutually contradictory;
they are all subsumed within the teaching that expresses and the principle and wisdom that are expressed.
And the obstacles to be severed are likened to a vajra.
The commentary on the fourth meaning states:
Furthermore, it is like the drawing of a vajra shape,
which is wide at the beginning and end but narrow in the middle;
such is the case with this Prajñāpāramitā.
The "narrow" refers to the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*);
the "broad" at the beginning and end refers to the Stage of Faithful Practice (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*) and the Stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgata-bhūmi*).
This demonstrates the meaning of the uncommon [teaching].

Based on this scriptural teaching.

Therefore, it is like a painted image of a Vajra deity:

To cause them to know the profound and subtle.
Question: Why is the Buddha-ground of extensive faith and practice explained in detail, while the purification of the mind is treated briefly?
Answer: The intent of this sutra is to cause one to resolve upon enlightenment and practice so that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed;
it extensively discusses the virtues of the fruition.
One encourages them to rejoice and be able to resolve their minds [on awakening],
for there is still the possibility of regression during the initial practice prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Thus,
the characteristics of the practice are extensively demonstrated.
This causes them to enter the first bhūmi and beyond,
because they have attained self-realization and are no longer subject to regression.
Since there is no need for extensive elaboration,
the beginning and the end are explained in detail while the middle is treated briefly.
Furthermore, from the stage of an ordinary being, one inherits the lineage of the Buddhas.
Thus, the principle that the fruit of Buddhahood arises without interruption is established;
the intermediate stages may be understood for themselves,
so what need is there for extensive explanation?
Therefore, the meaning of the scriptural text varies in its breadth and narrowness.
Although the explanation of the Tathāgata-bhūmi is subsumed within the ten stages (daśabhūmi), the sūtra does not explicitly clarify the specific characteristics of those ten stages.
It further refers to the fruit of Buddhahood;
all its merits are called the stage of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, this explanation is provided;
it shall be understood in detail below.
Question:
The *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"In the *prajñāpāramitā*, there is not a single dharma that can serve as a metaphor.

Answer: This reveals that his excellence in wisdom surpasses all phenomena,
such that nothing can serve as a complete analogy for comparison.
It is a small portion of that [vajra],
because its meaning and function are similar;
thus it is likened to a vajra.
Because those who possess wisdom understand through analogies, phenomena are clarified by means of metaphors;
their evidence is made manifest through prominent examples, thereby illustrating the boundaries of what has been perceived.
Realizing that which has not yet been seen,
they harmonize them into a single state,
causing their meanings to be equal.
All formal explanations are termed "illustrations" (dṛṣṭānta);
that is, by means of the manifest portion,
they clarify the unmanifest portion.
*Prajñā*, in the Sanskrit language, is translated here as "wisdom.
There are five types in total.
"Texts" refers to the teachings that serve as the means of expression.
The essence of the wisdom of contemplative observation is the true reality;
its sphere of genuine nature consists precisely of the two truths of emptiness and existence.
Regarding the three types of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) and so forth:

as for their "retinue" (*parivāra*), they consist of the four aggregates (*skandha*) associated with them, and as for their "companions" (*sahāya*), they consist of the five aggregates, as appropriate. This refers specifically to the two kinds of ethical discipline (*śīla*): that which is co-existent with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and that which is co-existent with the Path (*mārga*).
Therefore, because this name "prajñā" is broad and pervasive in its application,
its principle encompasses five types; yet,
from the perspective of what is preeminent, it refers specifically to the contemplation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
As explained in the treatise,
this wisdom is initially specific and subsequently universal.
Regarding the term "distinct characteristic" (pṛthak-lakṣaṇa):
it possesses the complete Sanskrit pronunciation and should be rendered as *pāra-kṣeya*.
This is translated as "wisdom" (hui).
In Sanskrit it is called *jñāna*,
which is translated here as "knowledge" (zhi).
Although their substance is the same—
both being wisdom directed toward specific objects—
their functional meanings differ.
Therefore, their names differ,
as the two types— discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and decisive resolution— are distinct.
This is based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, and other such texts.
If the term "letter" (akṣara) encompasses both the meanings of "cause" and "wisdom," then because these two characters,
*prajñā* (wisdom), constitute the realm (*dhātu*), the two characters *pra* and *ṇa* are its causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
When *prajñā* is assisted by *pā*, it becomes "wisdom" (*hui*);
when assisted by *jñā*, it becomes "knowledge" (*zhi*).
For this reason, among the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) in various sutras, [the distinction is made].
There are two distinct types of wisdom.
The *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The bodhisattva is fully endowed with prajñā."
"Endowed with jñāna.
It is also said:
"Attaining the gate of jñāna."
One is able to enter the gates of prajñā by discerning the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings and analyzing the meanings of phrases.
As for what is called the "common characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa):
Because their essence is identical,
wisdom is spoken of in the context of knowledge, and knowledge is spoken of in the context of wisdom.
There is no contradiction whatsoever.
Thus, the sixth is spoken of as "Prajñāpāramitā" (Perfection of Wisdom) and so forth.
Question:
The title is "Prajñāpāramitā" (Perfection of Wisdom).
Why, then, is giving explained within the context of the practices? Answer:
When the preceding [perfection] induces the subsequent, it is subsumed under the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*);

when the subsequent purifies the preceding, it is subsumed under the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). These are cited alternately as representative examples; in reality, they are similar. Furthermore, the names are established based on their predominant practice, and this is stated in reference to the initial stage.
The two bases of giving (*dāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are each mentioned separately. As for *pāra*:
This is called "the other shore.
Among the four aspects of the Dharma— principle, teaching, practice,
and fruit— it refers specifically to the fruit.
Taking bodhi and nirvāṇa as the "other shore," the doctrine and principle encompass both cause and effect,
while practice pertains solely to the cause.
Therefore, the suffering and its origin that have not yet arisen are regarded as the river;
the suffering and its origin currently arising are regarded as this shore;
and the six perfections are the boat.
It is precisely by means of the practitioner— the provisional entity consisting of the five aggregates— that one is delivered.
"Pāramitā" (Perfection) signifies the meaning of transcendence and the meaning of arrival.
By cultivating generosity and the other perfections,
one leaves birth and death behind and reaches the further shore.
In the ninth chapter on Consciousness-Only,
it is stated that the pāramitās can only be established when they are embraced by the seven kinds of supremacy.
First, the excellence of abiding securely,
which means one must abide securely within the bodhisattva lineage (*gotra*).
Second, the excellence of relying upon what is correct.
That is to say, one must rely upon the great bodhicitta,
which is the most excellent of the three types of intention;
specifically, it requires compassion for all sentient beings.
Fourth is the excellence of activity,
which means one must fully carry out all activities.
Fifth is the excellence of skillful means.
This means that it must be embraced by non-conceptual wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*);
this is the most excellent of the six types of dedication (*pariṇāmana*),
meaning that it must be dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The seventh is the most excellent purity,
meaning that one must not be interspersed with the two obstacles;
if it is not subsumed within these seven, it is not so.
The giving and other practices performed by the recipient do not constitute a perfection (pāramitā); it is by virtue of this [giving] and so forth [that the donor attains it].
Regarding each of the pāramitās,
one should apply a fourfold analysis (catuṣkoṭi) to each.
The second chapter of the Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra:
There are twelve supreme qualities;
therefore, all attain the further shore.
The eleventh [chapter], titled "Treatise on the Abhidharma," has five meanings.
It explains the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.
These are subsumed by five causes and conditions,
as explained in a separate chapter by the commentator on the Sūtra.
"Brahma-svara-sūtra" and "xiūgòulù" are both corruptions.
The correct term is *sūtra*.
Thus, four meanings are identified:
clothing, thread, matting, and scripture;
these are analogous to the name "Gau."
Śāṇakavāsin and others were instructed to take up the meaning of the sūtra and also to take up the meaning of the thread.
As the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"It is like various kinds of flowers placed upon a table;
when the wind blows, they scatter and fall."
By holding it with a swift thread, one prevents it from being lost or scattered.
The faculties and dispositions of sentient beings are like a table;
the Buddha’s spoken teachings and meanings are like flowers.
If they were not connected and maintained,
the winds of false views and delusions would have caused them to drift away and scatter;
now, the compilers of the canon have linked them together.
To string together the Buddha’s words is like using thread;
to thread the flowers is like weaving warp and weft.
As the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
The noble teachings penetrate and sustain both the meanings to be explained and the sentient beings to be converted;
these may be respectively correlated with the two meanings of the *sūtra* (the thread).
However, the characters of these scriptures are identical in name to those of the scriptural proclamations of this region.
According to the common interpretation here in this region,
"jing" (sūtra) means:
It is the eternal, the dharma, and the scripture.
Therefore, that which is not altered today is the eternal;
that which establishes the criteria for determining right and wrong is the law and the rule.
To penetrate the principles of phenomena is what constitutes a sūtra;
Buddhism is the same in this regard,
and there is no error therein.
In the treatises of the Hīnayāna,
the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* explains five meanings,
namely the meanings of "gushing spring" and so forth.
As has been stated previously, although the sūtras belong to the category of "teaching" (śāsana),
according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
they are established as the essence of the sūtra (*sūtratantra*).
Since this refers collectively to that which is expressed,
the term "sūtra" generally encompasses both the teaching and the principle;
likewise, the Prajñāpāramitā also encompasses both principle and teaching.
Based on this, there are four possible permutations when considering the relationship between the *sūtra* and the *samādhi*.
That is to say, "Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā" is a term where the *sūtra* and the *samādhi* share the same function (*karmadhāraya*);
it should be explained accordingly as either a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) or a *karmadhāraya*.
In explaining the text, first the structural analysis (viniścaya) is provided,
followed by the commentary.
This follows the analysis and interpretation of the Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
This sutra contains ten thematic points and eighteen loci;
the commentaries by the other two masters do not provide distinct structural divisions.
Thus says the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
The main body of the teaching is divided into four parts:
first, the entrustment through mindful protection;
second, the dwelling.
Third, the cultivation [of the three trainings]; fourth, the severing of doubts;
together with the introduction and the circulation [of the text], these constitute six sections.
Bodhiruci’s *Record of Vajrasattva* classifies [the teachings] into twelve categories,
each of which is extensive and manifold.
Since this is not the intended meaning of the treatise, it is not accepted here.
However, the Dharma Master Dao’an of the Jin dynasty...
The people of that time called him the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta;
he categorized and analyzed various sutras,
dividing them into three parts.
The introductory section,
the main body, and the dissemination section.
Later, he translated the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
This was originally composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva as a commentary on the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*;
its three parts are identical to this [present work].
Knowing that the wondrous principle penetrates in silence,
and that his enlightened mind merges mysteriously with the profound— how could the title "Pervading Heaven" (Miyen) be anything other than well-founded?
As for the "three divisions," they are:
first, the division on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching;
second, the division on what is taught in the holy scripture.
The third section, "Following the Teaching and Practicing It," differs slightly in name but not in its underlying meaning and principle;
according to this, the scriptural text is divided into three parts.
From the beginning up to "having spread out a seat, he sat down" constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*).
At that time, the Elder Subhūti was among the great assembly.
Up to the point where it says, "One should contemplate in this manner," constitutes the Main Body (zhengzongfen);
the remainder is termed the Dissemination (liutong).
The introduction consists of two parts.
The first is the general introduction,
namely "Thus have I heard," and so forth.
The subsequent separate narration is as follows:
"At that time, the World-Honored One... and so forth.
Within these two introductory sections, there are five pairs of names.
First, the correspondence between general and specific [teachings],
because various sūtras share commonalities while possessing distinct conditions for their respective sections.
Second, the correspondence between the introduction of faith and the origination [of the teaching].
The first transmitter of the Dharma cites evidence to inspire faith;
the subsequent expounder of the Dharma initiates the discourse through specific conditions.
This corresponds to the distinction between the postscript at the end of the sutra and the prologue at its beginning.
Because the teachings following the sūtra are inherently present before the sūtra;
the fourfold introduction by Ānanda and the introduction by the Tathāgata correspond to one another,
being designated as "explanation" (sūtra) because they are skillful means derived from [the Buddha's] request.
The five future sections correspond to the present section;
because Ānanda subsequently requested [the teaching], it concerns the causal origin (nidāna) of that time.
Thus, although there are many names, [it refers to this].
The first two [categories] correspond to names;
their principles and meanings are exhaustive and capable [of encompassing all],
yet each is given its two names according to what is predominant.
If it were not so, would the realization of its arising not be universal?
In order to explain the "Testimony of Faith" (samyak-pratyaya) of the general introduction,
one first analyzes it according to three gates.
First, the causes and conditions for their coexistence;
second, the rationale for their establishment;
third, the differences in their classification and synthesis.
As for the causes and conditions for its arising,
they are found in the Mahāmāyā Sūtra and the Mahākaruṇā Sūtra.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts describe these matters in detail;
however, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*...
Upāli instructed Ānanda to inquire about the Mahāsūtra and other texts;
Aniruddha provided instruction.
The two of them together instructed each other to raise one question each.
Regarding the inquiry on four matters:
first, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, whom shall the bhikṣus take as their teacher?
Second, upon what does it rely for its abiding?
Third, how should a bhikṣu of evil character be disciplined?
Fourth, what words should be placed at the beginning of all sūtras?
The Buddha said: "After my parinirvāṇa,
let the prātimokṣa be your great teacher."
Abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness,
one should treat a bhikṣu of evil character with the "Brahma-penance. It is called the Brahma-penance because it is characterized by silence.
One should not strike or revile others, but rather expel them through silence.
At the beginning of all sūtras, one should place the words "Thus have I heard" and so forth.
Question:
Why did Ānanda ask only four questions,
neither more nor less? Answer:
The precepts can restrain evil and may serve as a teacher;
by relying on them, one cultivates and studies the foundations of mindfulness to destroy perversions.
The silent Dharma of Brahma can subdue wicked people.
First, the correct practice is elucidated;
next, the correct understanding is elucidated;
and finally, the removal of hindrances is elucidated.
These three gateways must necessarily rely upon the sacred teachings;
thus, what is asked herein neither exceeds nor falls short [of them].
Furthermore, they cure the disease of birth and death.
One must possess four things:
first, a skilled physician;
second, the seeking of excellent medicine.
Third, the transgressions of the three consciousnesses;
fourth, the principles of the excellent sūtras and medical prescriptions.
These correspond respectively to the period after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the Great King of Physicians.
These four are essential;
therefore, they are asked about.
Furthermore, these constitute the non-interruption of the Three Jewels.
Taking the precepts as one's teacher is equivalent to the Buddha Jewel;
one must not sever ties with even a bhikṣu of evil character.
Once they have been disciplined,
the assembly attains harmony;
this is precisely the Saṅgha Jewel.

Question:
Having concluded the preceding section on the locus of the path of realization (*abhisamaya*) based on this treatise,

Answer: There are two explanations for this.
One says that this refers to all ten stages (*bhūmi*), because the "wondrous great body" (*mahākāya*) is said to pervade all ten stages.

If that is so, how is it that it was previously stated that the Stage of the Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*) is narrow at the beginning and broad at the end? Answer:
The preparatory practices and vows of the stages are vast and expansive,
and the fruit of Buddhahood is likewise so; however, within the ten stages, one seeks the subsequent stage with proximity, practicing in a limited manner and in a single mode,
cultivating and realizing each stage individually— therefore, it is called "narrow."

One interpretation holds that the "pure mind" refers exclusively to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),

It is named the "Ultimate Ground" (niṣṭhā-bhūmi) by way of its fruit;

Cultivating the six perfections is like seeing and cultivating them simultaneously; upon seeing the principle,

If all ten stages were already states of pure mind (*viśuddha-citta*),
what further would there be to do after the stage of the pure mind-ground?

Sūtra: Subhūti arrives at the contemplation of the Tathāgata. Commentary:
The fourth [section] concerns the grasping of the Dharma-body.
Although the previous section concerning the state of perfect enlightenment deals with the *dharmakāya*, it does not explicitly and fully clarify the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Because this [section] clarifies the *dharmakāya* by manifesting the cause of unsurpassed awakening as being unsurpassed, it is explained here.
Furthermore, the preceding section explained both the Dharma-body and the Reward-body together;
since the Dharma-body is the fundamental basis,
this [section] clarifies it now so that one may grasp it through correct contemplation and correct realization.
For those who wish to attain the form-body (rūpakāya),
although they abide in the midst of clarity regarding the dharma-body (dharmakāya),
because they seek the form-body, they are made to rejoice in the true principle without grasping at signs; thus it is taught.
This is because they desire to obtain a dwelling place for the form-body (rūpakāya) rather than the dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Their desires are poles apart from those who seek the three kinds of verbal expression and merit elucidated within the dharma-body.
The Dharma-body of the characteristic of wisdom is what clearly elucidates the characteristic of wisdom;
it also distinguishes the unconditioned, yet it does not correctly clarify the principle.
As for making offerings to and attending upon the Tathāgata’s dwelling place:
Although it clarifies the signless (*animitta*),
that was explained in reference to the Buddha-body to which offerings are made, not as clarifying what one has personally attained.
Now, clarifying what one has personally attained also clarifies the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Buddha-ground sought above, so that one may cause it to be personally grasped.
Furthermore, this passage exists because the *dharmakāya* is not known through signs, nor is it obtained by means of the causes of merit characterized by signs;
thus, the intent of that treatise is likewise to sever the doubt regarding the second and twenty-second [point], namely, the doubt concerning the nature of the *dharma* as being inferable.
Furthermore, regarding the severance of the twenty-third mark, which is the cause for the formation of merit,
the treatise says:
"Again, there is doubt."
Although one cannot perceive the Tathāgata through the accomplishment of his marks,
for he does not have those as his essence;
rather, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is his essence.
Since the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is established through the perfection of marks and signs,
one may infer that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is perfected by the marks of merit.
The following scriptural passage serves to resolve this doubt.
Yan said: "This passage sets forth two doubts.
The first is that although the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body cannot be accomplished through marks..."
It should be stated that direct realization can be inferred through the accomplishment of the marks.
Second, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata should be attained through the accomplishment of the marks of merit.
Below this, the treatise contains three lines of verse.
The first and last verses answer the first doubt,
while the single intermediate verse answers the second doubt;
however, this intermediate verse as well as the various prose sections [further elaborate].
This verse-text should have been explained later when clarifying the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the accomplishment of the marks; however,
the author of the treatise has placed it here because these two points of doubt are interconnected.
The preceding introduction raised the doubt by posing the questions together;

Furthermore, since the example of the universal monarch (*cakravartin*) is analogous, scholars of both ancient and modern times have maintained that the translation is erroneous.
This reasoning is not necessarily correct;

This means that while one sees physical forms and hears the sound of the Dharma being preached, these are the conventional truth; because it is the true reality of the Dharmakāya, it cannot be seen.

"How am I to be seen? For this reason, one should give rise to true contemplation herein and contemplate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

In order to eliminate this attachment, the Sūtra says: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to give away the seven treasures... [Commentary: It is said: The meaning is as follows: Although a bodhisattva may possess great wealth and provide for the needs of all sentient beings, if they harbor thoughts of attachment toward these things, they will not attain liberation from saṃsāra. Therefore, the Buddha taught that one should practice giving with a mind free from attachment, even if it be only the gift of a single flower. This is because such a mind is capable of generating the roots of goodness for attaining supreme enlightenment. Furthermore, although the aforementioned seven treasures are vast and immeasurable, they are still conditioned phenomena; thus, they cannot bring about the attainment of the unconditioned Dharma-body. Consequently, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate the perfection of giving by relinquishing even one's own body and life. This is because, through such a mind, one can generate the roots of goodness for attaining supreme enlightenment. Moreover, although the aforementioned seven treasures are vast and immeasurable, they are still subject to destruction and decay. Thus, they cannot bring about the attainment of the indestructible and undecaying Dharma-treasure. Consequently, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate the perfection of giving by relinquishing even one's own head, eyes, marrow, and brain. This is because, through such a mind, one can generate the roots of goodness for attaining supreme enlightenment. Furthermore, although the aforementioned seven treasures are vast and immeasurable, they are still subject to loss and exhaustion. Thus, they cannot bring about the attainment of the inexhaustible Dharma-treasure. Consequently, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate the perfection of giving by relinquishing even one's own hands and feet. This is because, through such a mind, one can generate the roots of goodness for attaining supreme enlightenment. Moreover, although the aforementioned seven treasures are vast and immeasurable, they are still subject to transformation and change. Thus, they cannot bring about the attainment of the immutable Dharma-treasure. Consequently, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate the perfection of giving by relinquishing even one's own wife and children. This is because, through such a mind, one can generate the roots of goodness for attaining supreme enlightenment. Furthermore, although the aforementioned seven treasures are vast and immeasurable, they are still subject to the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death. Thus, they cannot bring about the attainment of the state free from birth, aging, sickness, and death. Consequently, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate the perfection of giving by relinquishing even one's own kingdom, ministers, and retinue. This is because, through such a mind, one can generate the roots of goodness for attaining supreme enlightenment. Moreover, although the aforementioned seven treasures are vast and immeasurable, they are still subject to the suffering of being born into the three evil realms. Thus, they cannot bring about the attainment of the state free from birth in the three evil realms. Consequently, the Buddha taught that one should cultivate the perfection of giving by relinquishing even one's own country, city, and capital. This is because, through such a mind, one can generate the roots of goodness for attaining supreme enlightenment. Furthermore, although the aforementioned seven treasures are vast and immeasurable, they are still subject to the suffering of being born into the eight difficult conditions. "Observing the objects of the sphere of Avalokiteśvara, their transience, movement, and essential nature..."
The youthful, the flourishing, and the long-lived creators— contemplating the mind and its presence or absence,
they observe with mastery.
They are like stars and other celestial bodies reflected in the sky, moving through their courses according to the directions.
Their radiance and color are intensely brilliant;
even if they were to endure for a long time, they would ultimately perish at the end of the kalpa.
Such are the various meritorious rewards experienced by humans and devas.
Abundant wealth and high status are objects of universal admiration;
yet though one may long enjoy sovereign power, it ultimately returns to emptiness.
One should contemplate all objective phenomena as being like visual distortions.
For example, just as one with cataracts sees hair-whirls, floating flowers, or a second moon in the clear sky,
so too is it with consciousness clouded by ignorance;
within the reality of suchness, where no thing exists, [it perceives things that are not there].
He perceives the various phenomena of the internal and external, mundane and supramundane,
as shifting and moving like a lamp;
for example, like the flame of a lamp.
It perishes as soon as it arises and does not reach another place;
nevertheless, because of this flame, another flame arises in another place,
as if there were a movement.
The aggregates are likewise;
observing their essential nature to be like an illusion,
they manifest in the form of a woman.
One should contemplate that their essential nature is non-existent;
yet those who do not understand take them to be real.
All phenomena are likewise so.
Contemplate the prime of youth as being like dew;
when the sun appears, the dew dries away,
and so too do the complexion and beauty of one's flourishing years.
Once encountered by impermanence, one passes away;
observe that life is like a bubble,
just as a bubble upon water.
Some are born with their physical forms and characteristics as yet unformed;
others, having just been born, or having remained for a brief moment, immediately return to destruction.
The same applies to their lifespan and birth.
From the initial formation of the womb until the decay of old age and final destruction,
one contemplates the agent as being like a dream;
within the dream, one follows what was previously seen or heard.
Because the habitual tendencies of recollective discrimination abide within it,
although there is no agent, various objects appear before one;
this is because the habitual tendencies of afflictions and karma from beginningless time abide within it.
Although there is no "self" that acts as an agent,
the boundless phenomena of birth, death, and so forth nevertheless manifest;
contemplate the mind as being like lightning.
That which arises perishes immediately; every moment must pass away. Contemplate existence and non-existence as being like clouds:
like clouds in the sky, they were previously absent and later appear, changing and vanishing in an instant.
Conditioned phenomena are likewise thus:
their essential nature is fundamentally empty, existing only through delusive conditions;
once those conditions disperse, they return once more to non-existence.

these may serve as general metaphors for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) or as specific metaphors for individual dharmas.
The examples cited here are specific illustrations; however,
according to the two treatises, it is correct to state that there are nine metaphors,
whereas this sutra lacks four of them.
The [Tibetan] version includes "star," "lamp," and "cloud," while adding the metaphor of "shadow";
the Liang edition omits "star" and adds "darkness."
Because the starlight appears in the darkness,
it may be that the translator’s intention differed or the Sanskrit manuscripts were distinct, making them impossible to reconcile.
Seventh, regarding the explanation of the excellence of the benefits through analogies:
Because one practices this contemplation according to the exposition of this treatise,
one becomes free from defiled attachment to the conditioned flow of saṃsāra and thereby attains liberation.
If that is so, then all nine contemplations lead to liberation.
Why are only the latter three called "renunciation"?
Answer: In truth, all of them are capable of attaining renunciation.
However, the preceding analogy specifically clarifies another meaning: here,
the sense of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*) regarding persons and phenomena is augmented, and it also accords with the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*),
because that very aspect of transcendence is what is being contemplated.
Therefore, it is said: The verse in that treatise states:
"Observing characteristics and experiencing [their results], one observes the events of the three periods of time."
Having completed the detailed analysis regarding the attainment of stainless sovereignty over conditioned phenomena,
I shall next explain the scriptural text.
The first line presents the principle;
the next two lines provide the analogy;
and the final line offers the exhortation.
[Sutra]: After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, [the assembly] received it with faith and practiced accordingly. Commentary:
The section on dissemination (parīndanā) consists of three parts.
First, the Buddha’s transformation is concluded;
next, it clarifies that the assembly heard it together;
finally, the meaning of their joyful faith and acceptance by the upāsakas and others is as explained in the usual manner.
According to the scriptures of the Wei and Zhou dynasties, there are Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
the *Zhenguan* edition quotes all eight sections in full,
whereas this text is abbreviated.
This treatise states in verse:
"If one hears such a Dharma as this, yet lacks awakening regarding the Great Vehicle, their self-attachment exceeds that of a stone; for ultimately, there is no cause [for its removal]."
Ordinary people, regarding this profound and great Dharma, are unable to awaken to it, know it, or have faith and inclination toward it;
worldly beings are for the most part like this. For this reason, this Dharma has fallen into desuetude.
Thus it was proclaimed.
The first verse clarifies that those who lack awakening and understanding possess no cause for bodhi;
the subsequent verse clarifies that because they do not have faith and inclination, the Dharma becomes extinguished.
The former is intended to inspire the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment.
Later, wishing for the Dharma to endure for a long time,
that treatise’s verse says:
The rare dharmas of the total retention of all Buddhas, Whose profound words and meanings are beyond measure.
"Having heard from the Venerable One and having heard the extensive exposition...
These two upper lines praise the extraordinary excellence of the Buddha’s Dharma;
the following line continues the lineage and transmits the lamp.
The following line expresses the vow of dedication and transfer.
Regarding those who joyfully practice this,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
It is for the sake of generating wisdom.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"There are three kinds of meanings through which one joyfully practices and upholds [the teaching]."
Some say that the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra* is also the same;
this statement should be examined.
One explanation is that purity arises from attaining mastery over all phenomena.
The first clarifies that one is not defiled by grasping at gain and honor;
the second clarifies that what is taught is pure because it knows the essence of the pure dharma as it truly is.
This means that the teaching of the realized truth is free from false attachments, and thus the doctrine, the principles, and the capacities of the listeners are all in accord.
Furthermore, because it possesses the ten kinds of purity and excellence, such as being virtuous in the beginning,
middle, and end, one attains three kinds of pure fruits.
This clarifies that the recipient, according to the three aspects of the object, the practice, and the fruit as they were taught, [attains these results].
They rejoice because they have initiated practice and attained the realization of that objective;
for as the listeners' faculties are suitable to hear it, the Buddha preaches correctly for them, and none fail to believe and awaken.
Having received this and held it in mind, one reverently practices and trains accordingly;
for this reason, it is said that "with joy, one accepts and practices.
This sublime principle is not to be fathomed by the ignorant; relying upon this treatise, I have briefly expounded it.
